You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC rule induction

When test input appearance encourages an unverified transformation or demos suggest a global operation:
1. Treat task IDs, memory, and resemblance as priors only; confirm current evidence.
2. Without a grounded matching rule, request a demonstration instead of guessing. Seek examples that distinguish hypotheses.
3. Compare the complete input/output pair: dimensions, every changed cell, rows, columns, colors, and output regularities. Do not assume dominant test-object geometry controls the transformation.
4. State a rule that explains the whole demo and verify it against every cell before applying to the test.
5. Emit exactly one valid Continual-ARC JSON action, without prose.

Case note: task-a29c068e yielded no successful rule despite 8 submissions. Demos were structurally mixed: several sparse clusters stayed unchanged, while one bg5 and one bg7 arrangement received multiple diagonal rays in differing colors/directions. The bg1 demo extended 9 down-right. Test bg4 had markers 7 at (4,7),(5,8), 8 at (5,9),(6,9),(7,10), and 6 at (6,8),(7,7). Eight guesses failed (unchanged, individual rays, diagonal staircases, extrapolated multi-ray/color ideas). No transformation was established. Treat the examples as insufficient to infer the test; do not repeat guessed ray/cascade behavior without matching structural evidence.

Pitfall: sparse, compelling test markers can be irrelevant to the task rule. A demo may reveal a periodic or row-wise global output; analyze the whole grid.
